advisor_letter:
Dear [[CLIENT_NAME]],

You are two years from a threshold, and at this stage the next three to five years carry more weight than the next thirty. The choices made on the cusp of retirement set the rhythm for everything that follows, and I sense that what matters most to you and [[SPOUSE_NAME]] is knowing that the life you have built together will hold once the paycheques stop.

The two of you arrive here having assembled a little over half a million dollars across registered and non-registered accounts, with public benefits forming the backbone of your future income. You have made the structural choice to plan as a couple, and you carry one significant mortgage into this transition — a piece of the picture that shapes how the rest fits together.

This report is built to give you clarity rather than topics. The executive summary delivers the verdict in thirty seconds. Chapter I lays out the foundations and the projection of where your wealth could travel. Chapter II describes the risk you would be taking and where the plan feels its strain. Chapter III walks through the strategies and decisions that could shift the trajectory, and Chapter IV offers alternatives worth testing before you commit. I encourage particular attention to Chapter III, because that is where the mortgage and your spending pace could be examined together.

None of what follows is a verdict on your effort, which has plainly been considerable. It is a map of what the numbers suggest could happen and what might change the odds. Read it as a conversation we are beginning, not a conclusion handed down.

Warmly, your BuildFi analyst. Consult a certified financial planner before acting on any observation in this report.
overall_assessment: Your plan lands at a **60%** success rate — a grade of C, under strain but far from broken. The clearest strength is the public-benefit floor, which would cover **72%** of your guaranteed income needs and steady the household through most futures. The main pressure point is the mortgage you carry into retirement: at a debt-to-savings ratio near half, it competes directly with the savings meant to fund your spending. One observation that could move the picture most is the pace of withdrawals against that debt, since the structure of the mortgage appears to be the single lever with the longest reach here.
verdict: A success rate in genuinely mixed territory means more futures hold than fail, but the margin is thin. The median scenario would leave roughly **32K$** in real wealth at the horizon, while the cautious scenario reaches **$0** — meaning savings could be fully drawn down before life's end in the less favourable half of outcomes. That spread, with a favourable scenario near **182K$**, shows a plan whose result depends heavily on how the early retirement years unfold.
page_zero_verdict: What seems to weigh on you both is whether the savings will outlast you while a mortgage still sits on the books — a fair concern for a couple standing two years from retirement. This report is here to show you where that worry is grounded and where it eases.
profile_summary: Across your household you hold **560K$** in total savings — **295K$** in RRSPs, **58K$** in TFSAs, and **22K$** in non-registered accounts — a reasonable spread across registered and taxable buckets. The portfolio sits at roughly 55.5% equity and 44.5% bonds, a balance that suits a couple on the edge of retirement. The diversification across account types gives you flexibility in how income could be drawn.
trajectory_insight: The projection points toward a median real wealth of **32K$** at the horizon, with a favourable path reaching **182K$** and a cautious path settling at **$0**. The wide gap between these reflects how much the order of early returns and your spending pace would govern the outcome. In the cautious half of futures the trajectory crosses zero before the horizon, which is why the plan reads as under strain rather than comfortable.
income_insight: Public benefits would cover **72%** of your guaranteed income, a strong floor anchored by QPP/CPP as the dominant source alongside OAS. Against monthly spending, a gap of about $2,217 remains to be funded from personal savings each month. That gap is modest relative to the floor, but it is the part of the income picture most sensitive to how long the portfolio lasts.
taxInsight: Over the full horizon the plan would carry roughly **321K$** in lifetime tax, against an average effective rate near 13.3% — a moderate burden that reflects income drawn largely from registered accounts. OAS clawback does not appear in any year, so there is no recovery tax eroding your benefits at these income levels. The most influential lever here is the ordering of withdrawals across RRSP, TFSA, and non-registered accounts, where a more deliberately sequenced draw could surface meaningful tax savings over time. As Alberta applies a flatter provincial bracket structure than Quebec, your marginal exposure stays comparatively contained across the retirement years. A certified financial planner could model the sequencing in detail.
estateInsight: The projection points to a net estate of about **55K$** in the median scenario, with **$0** in tax at death — a reflection of modest remaining registered balances and Alberta's flat probate ceiling. Because you plan as a couple, assets would roll to the surviving spouse before any deemed disposition applies. The estate is genuinely a residual here rather than a planning objective.
gis_insight: The model shows eligibility for the Guaranteed Income Supplement across roughly 8 years, contributing about 17K$ in lifetime GIS to the household. GIS sits as a complement to your CPP/OAS floor at lower-income stretches, not as a destination the plan relies upon. It carries a 50-cent-per-dollar reduction as other income rises, so the benefit naturally tapers in years when withdrawals lift your income above the threshold.
debt_insight: You carry a single mortgage of **285K$** into retirement, putting your debt-to-savings ratio near 51% — meaning roughly half of what you have saved is mirrored by what you owe. None of this is high-rate debt, which removes the urgency that consumer balances would create, yet the mortgage remains the structural lever in this plan. At its 5.4% rate, the balance carries an interest cost near $15,000 a year at the outset — money that would otherwise stay invested, and a figure that would shrink with each year of scheduled paydown. How and when the mortgage is carried or retired would shape the withdrawal pressure on your portfolio more than any other single factor, and examining it alongside your spending pace could reveal the most room to ease the strain.
riskInsight: The spread between the cautious scenario at **$0** and the favourable one at **182K$** is wide, and savings show durability only to about age 76 in the median path before depletion pressure builds. The factor that matters most here is the sequence of returns in the first retirement years, since a weak start would compound against the withdrawals needed to cover the income gap. This is the zone where small adjustments to spending would have the largest effect.
stress_interpretation: The plan is most vulnerable to a sustained spending increase, where success falls to 18% — a steep drop from the baseline — and to a longevity extension, which pulls it to 33%. It holds up comparatively better under persistent inflation, where success stays near 54%. The pattern indicates a plan governed more by spending discipline and lifespan than by market shocks alone, which points to behaviour as the lever with the steadiest grip on the outcome.
